summary: Describes a mechanism for signaling active or standby status of redundant pseudowires between their end points, so provider edge nodes agree on which one carries traffic. It applies to single-segment and multi-segment pseudowires.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC adds status information for sets of backup pseudowires. Endpoints can tell each other which path should carry user traffic and can request a coordinated switch.

questions: what is the pseudowire preferential forwarding status bit
how does pw redundancy choose the active pseudowire
what is independent mode vs master slave mode pseudowire
subtitle: A pair of status bits helps pseudowire endpoints coordinate active paths and switching.

tldr.problem: When multiple pseudowires provide backup paths, both endpoints need a shared way to select which path carries user traffic.
tldr.mechanism: A Preferential Forwarding bit reports active or standby state, and a Request Switchover bit can request a coordinated move to another pseudowire.
tldr.outcome: The RFC defines independent and master/slave modes and updates RFC 4447. RFC 7771 later updates this RFC.

today: RFC 6870 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 4447 and is updated by RFC 7771.

sections.title: Why Redundant Pseudowires Need Status
sections.content:
A redundant pseudowire set can contain several paths between provider-edge endpoints. When more than one path is available, each endpoint needs to use the same path for user traffic. The existing status codes report faults, but do not identify the preferred forwarding path.

This RFC adds a Preferential Forwarding status bit and a Request Switchover status bit. It supports 1:1 and N:1 protection, but not 1+1 protection that duplicates traffic continuously on both paths.
sections.plainLanguage: Backup paths work only when both ends agree on which one carries user data. The new status bits provide a way to share that choice and request a change.

sections.title: Independent Mode
sections.content:
In independent mode, each endpoint selects which pseudowires it considers active and advertises that state. A pseudowire carries user traffic only when it is up and both endpoints indicate active. If either endpoint indicates standby, neither forwards user data over it.

If multiple paths qualify, both endpoints need a common selection rule. The required default selects the lowest PWid for a PWid FEC; for a Generalized PWid FEC, endpoints compare the specified identifier triplet. Local precedence or primary and secondary designations may also be used.
sections.plainLanguage: Each endpoint reports its own choice. A path carries user data only when both ends report it as active.

sections.title: Master and Slave Roles
sections.content:
In master/slave mode, one endpoint chooses the active pseudowire and the other follows its status. The master advertises active or standby and ignores the status it receives from the slave. Roles are set by local configuration.

The RFC does not define how to detect incorrect role configuration or provide a backup master. When node protection is required, it recommends independent mode.
sections.plainLanguage: The master chooses the path and tells the slave what to use. This mode depends on correct local role configuration.

sections.title: Requesting a Coordinated Switch
sections.content:
An endpoint may set the Request Switchover bit on the pseudowire it wants to use. It waits for the peer's acknowledgment before activating that path. The waiting timer should be configurable and defaults to 3 seconds.

The peer acknowledges by reporting the requested path as active, then updates the old path to standby. A request for a down path is ignored. If both endpoints request a switch at once, their system IP addresses determine which request is handled as the receiver's request.
sections.plainLanguage: An endpoint can ask to move traffic and wait for the peer to confirm. After confirmation, both endpoints update which path is active.

sections.title: Compatibility, Security and Status Codes
sections.content:
Both endpoints must negotiate the PW Status TLV before using these mechanisms. An implementation that does not recognize the new bits must ignore them. For multi-segment pseudowires, switching provider-edge nodes relay status notifications between segments.

The RFC applies the security considerations of the base pseudowire setup protocol and says a redundant set is only as secure as its least-secure member. IANA assigned 0x00000020 for Preferential Forwarding and 0x00000040 for Request Switchover.
sections.plainLanguage: Older endpoints can ignore status bits they do not understand. The security of the entire backup set depends on every pseudowire in that set.
